title: 1MW No. 318: Every Yes Has a Cost
author: Greg McKeown
summary: Greg McKeown's weekly "1-Minute Wednesday" essay uses Starbucks' simultaneous push for mobile-order convenience and coffeehouse connection -- a strategy Michael Porter would call "straddling," pursuing two incompatible priorities through the same limited resources -- as a case study in what happens when leaders refuse to make trade-offs. McKeown extends the diagnosis to individuals: adding a new project without naming what will stop, or promising presence at home while letting work consume the evening, are the personal version of Starbucks' problem. He cites a 2026 study by Sarah Memmi and Jordan Etkin (12 experiments on multi-goal pursuit) showing that people who set goals before budgeting their available time consistently over-commit, while those who allocate time first set more realistic goals and report more progress and satisfaction. The essay's actionable takeaway is a single question to ask before any new commitment: what will I have to say no to in order to say yes to this -- because every yes has a cost, and the Essentialist's job is to choose that cost deliberately rather than let circumstances choose it later.
points: McKeown frames Starbucks' simultaneous push for both mobile-order speed and coffeehouse connection as a textbook case of what Michael Porter calls "straddling": pursuing two strategies without accepting either one's trade-offs, using the same baristas and the same minutes for both.

A 2026 study by Memmi and Etkin (12 experiments) found that people who set goals before budgeting their time systematically over-commit, while those who allocate time first before setting goals make more realistic plans and report more progress and satisfaction.

His practical rule is to ask, before any new commitment, "what will I have to say no to in order to say yes to this" -- treating a blank answer as a signal to look harder rather than proof the addition is free.

The essay's central claim, echoed in the closing Rolheiser quote, is that every choice is a renunciation, and trade-offs refused voluntarily get made involuntarily by one's calendar, health, or relationships instead.
quotes: By 2025, mobile orders were arriving faster than customers could get to the store. Baristas were trying to keep up with a stream of digital orders while also serving the customers standing directly in front of them.

There was nothing wrong with either idea. Convenience mattered, and connection mattered. The problem was trying to maximize both at the same time, through the same baristas, the same counters, and the same minutes.
Michael Porter calls this straddling: pursuing two different strategies without accepting the trade-offs required by either.
When people set their goals first, they tended to commit to more than their available time could realistically support. In effect, we give the same hour away more than once.
But when participants divided their available time before setting their goals, their goals became more realistic. They made more progress and were happier with the outcome.
Before saying yes to something new, ask: What will I have to say no to in order to say yes to this? If the answer is nothing, look again. Every yes costs something.
